# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

# Umbraco schema through MCP

Every call goes to the `umbraco` server. Arguments are objects and arrays, never strings of JSON. Read each thing back after you create it.

## Built-in data types (same IDs on every default install)

| Data type | ID |
|---|---|
| Textstring | 0cc0eba1-9960-42c9-bf9b-60e150b429ae |
| Textarea | c6bac0dd-4ab9-45b1-8e30-e4b619ee5da3 |
| Rich text | ca90c950-0aff-4e72-b976-a30b1ac57dad |
| Image media picker | ad9f0cf2-bda2-45d5-9ea1-a63cfc873fd3 |
| Date picker | 5046194e-4237-453c-a547-15db3a07c4e1 |

Other data types: `find-data-type` or `get-all-data-types`. Don't create a new Textstring.

## Order

blocks → Block Grid data type → templates → page types → allowed children and templates → read everything back.

## Blocks (element types)

`create-element-type`:
```json
{"name": "Rich Text Block", "alias": "richTextBlock", "icon": "icon-document-html",
 "properties": [{"name": "Text", "alias": "text", "dataTypeId": "ca90c950-0aff-4e72-b976-a30b1ac57dad", "tab": "Content"}]}
```
Every property needs `name`, `alias`, `dataTypeId` and `tab`. A block with no properties is useless.

Filing into a folder (`move-document-type`): the target is an object.
```json
{"id": "<element type id>", "data": {"target": {"id": "<folder id>"}}}
```

## Block Grid data type

`create-data-type`. **editorAlias is `Umbraco.BlockGrid`.** `Umb.PropertyEditorUi.BlockGrid` is the UI alias, and as editorAlias it fails with "property editor was not found".
```json
{"name": "Blog Block Grid", "editorAlias": "Umbraco.BlockGrid", "editorUiAlias": "Umb.PropertyEditorUi.BlockGrid",
 "values": [
   {"alias": "gridColumns", "value": 12},
   {"alias": "blocks", "value": [
     {"contentElementTypeKey": "<block id>", "allowAtRoot": true, "allowInAreas": true}
   ]}
 ]}
```
Read it back with `get-data-type`. Its `blocks` value must list every block, or editors can't add any.

## Templates

`create-template` with `name` and `alias` only. Umbraco writes `Views/<alias>.cshtml`, and you fill in that same file later. Never move, rename or copy it.

## Document types (pages)

`create-document-type`: `name`, `alias`, `icon`, `parentId` (a folder, or leave it out for the root), and `properties` in the same shape as for blocks. A block grid property uses your Block Grid data type's ID.

## Allowed children and templates (`update-document-type`)

This replaces the whole document type. A half object fails validation or wipes properties.

1. `get-document-type-by-id`.
2. Send back **everything you got**, changing only:
   - `allowedTemplates`: `[{"id": "<template id>"}]`
   - `defaultTemplate`: `{"id": "<template id>"}`
   - `allowedDocumentTypes`: `[{"documentType": {"id": "<child type id>"}, "sortOrder": 0}]`

Do this for **the parent of your top page too** (the site root type must allow your front page type). Otherwise `create-page` fails with "Operation not permitted", which means "not an allowed child here".

Allowed children belong to the parent: the front page type allows the post type, and the root type allows the front page type.

Base directory for this skill: C:\code\benchmark\Umbraco.Bench\.claude\skills\umbraco-content # Umbraco content through MCP Pages, blocks and publishing go through `umbraco-editor`; media and domains go through `umbraco`. Keep the returned ID. 2. `create-media-multiple`: ```json {"sourceType": "filePath", "parentId": "", "files": [{"name": "Circuit board", "filePath": "C:/code/site/photos/circuit-board.jpg", "mediaTypeName": "Image"}]} ``` `filePath` is absolute, and it must be inside the folders the server allows (`UMBRACO_ALLOWED_MEDIA_PATHS`). ## Pages (`umbraco-editor`) Find the parent with `list-children` or `search-content`. `create-page`: ```json {"name": "Why MCP is awesome", "documentTypeId": "", "parentId": "", "values": [{"alias": "title", "value": "Why MCP is awesome"}, {"alias": "publishDate", "value": "2026-10-01T09:00:00"}]} ``` "Operation not permitted" means this type isn't an allowed child of the parent. Fix that with update-document-type on the parent's type (see the umbraco-schema skill). ### Value shapes - **Text, textarea:** a string. - **Date:** `2026-10-01T09:00:00`. - **Media picker:** a list with one entry, using a new GUID as `key`: ```json [{"key": "", "mediaKey": "", "mediaTypeAlias": "Image", "crops": [], "focalPoint": null}] ``` - **Rich text:** an object, not a string: ```json {"markup": "

First paragraph.

", "blocks": {"layout": {}, "contentData": [], "settingsData": [], "expose": []}} ``` ## Blocks in a block grid (`add-blockgrid-block`) One call per block, in reading order: ```json {"id": "", "propertyAlias": "body", "contentTypeKey": "", "values": [{"alias": "text", "value": {"markup": "

...

value.markup:
Before Model Context Protocol, wiring an AI assistant to your software meant building a bespoke integration for every pair: this assistant, that database, this design tool, that CMS. It was the n×m problem — every new player multiplied the work.

MCP collapses it to n+m. An assistant learns one protocol; a tool implements one server; and suddenly they all speak to each other. The tool describes its capabilities, the assistant discovers them at runtime, and no one writes glue code for a specific pairing ever again.

The best part is what it feels like in practice. An assistant that could only chat can now create a document type in your CMS, upload an image, publish a page — with permissions and confirmations you control. This very blog was built that way: schema, content and publishing all done through tool calls against Umbraco's MCP servers.
